examples: Anyone can apply, regardless of age.
People should be treated equally regardless of nationality.

fields.explain:
A normative/policy nuance, leaning toward written language, announcements, guidelines and regulations.
The second clause usually states something that holds for every case: “～できる/～とする/～は同じだ”.
Nのいかんによらず is more formal than Nによらず ; used in business/official contexts.
Not used when the result really does “depend” on N. When it depends, use ～によって/～次第で.

• Meaning: “Regardless of/not depending on/without regard to N, the result/condition stays the same”.
• Scope of N: age, gender, nationality, experience, weather, method, reason…
• Used to state general principles, policies, regulations, or general statements.
• The form Nのいかんによらず emphasizes all-inclusiveness and is very formal (announcements, contracts).
• Usually accompanied by a main clause meaning “allowed/not allowed/unchanged/applies to all/free of charge…”.
fields.notes:
• “によらず” is the negative form of “～による” (based on/depending on), meaning “not based on/not depending on”.
• “いかん” = 如何 (state/how things turn out). Fixed phrases:「天候のいかん」「成績のいかん」.
• Works well in regulatory texts: “～は、理由のいかんによらず、～とする”.
mistakes: Confusing “～によらず” with “～によって”. Incorrect example: 年齢によって誰でも応募できる (wrong meaning). Correct: 年齢によらず誰でも応募できる.
Using “によらず” when the actual result does depend on something → unnatural. When there is dependence, use “によって/次第で”.
Writing “いかん” incorrectly as “如何に” in this structure. Correct: Nのいかんによらず.
JLPT: trick questions often compare it with “～を問わず/～にかかわらず”. All three mean “regardless of”, but the formal nuance and the combination with “いかん” belong to “によらず”.

rows: More common in spoken language; wide scope, less formal than “いかんによらず”.

examples: Prior to the start of construction, we will hold a briefing session for the neighborhood.

fields.explain:
Formal; used in official documents, announcements and ceremonies.
Emphasizes the “preparation” for an important event/activity.
Not used for everyday chores: “食事に先立ち手を洗う” sounds too formal; 前に is more natural.

Expresses “before (an important matter) takes place, carrying out the preparation/related step”. Formal usage, suited to ceremonial, business and official-announcement settings. Implies necessary preparation, unlike “前に”, which simply indicates a point in time.
fields.notes:
• With verbs, the dictionary form (V辞書形) is usually used to nominalize the intended event: “発表するに先立ち”.
• Suitable for company templates: “導入に先立ち、～をご案内いたします”.
• In speeches, the fixed pair “に先立ち、簡単ではございますが…” is very natural.
meaning_vi: Before (carrying out a major undertaking)…, on the eve of…
examples: 1. ①　会議に先立って、メンバーの紹介が行われます。
2. ②　試合を始めるのに先立って、ルールの説明が行われます。
examples: 1. 選手団の出発に先立って、激励会が開かれた。
Before the team of athletes departed, a send-off rally was held to encourage them.
2. 記者会見に先立ち、講演要旨が配られた。
Before the press conference, a summary of the lecture was handed out.
3. 「試合開始に先立ち、国歌を演奏いたします」
“Before the start of the match, the national anthem will be performed”
4. 今回のケースでは、噴火に先立つ地震が４８時間続いた。
In this case, before the volcano erupted, earthquakes continued for 48 hours.
5. 駅前の再開発を進めるに先だって、住民の意見を聞く会が開かれた。
Before proceeding with the redevelopment in front of the station, a meeting to hear residents' opinions was held.
explain: Has the meaning of preparing in advance before ～. N is a word for an important event.
examples: 1. 開店に先立ち、関係者だけのパーティーが行われた。
Before the restaurant opened, a party for those involved only was held.
2. 新製品の開発に先立って、アンケート調査を行った。
Before developing the new product, a questionnaire survey was conducted.
mistakes: Using it for everyday matters makes the sentence too stiff → choose “前に”.
Forgetting to switch to the modifier form before N: “に先立つN”.
Confusing it with “にあたって”: exam questions often test the nuance of “preparing beforehand” (に先立ち) vs “on the occasion of starting” (にあたって).

fields.explain:
Placed before nouns denoting a point in time/major event:開幕・発売・公開・導入・実施・改正…
A promotional/official nuance; often seen in news headlines, plans and press releases.
Used for preparatory actions, announcements, trial runs, introductions… that take place before the main milestone.
If you simply mean “before” without emphasizing “pioneering”, use ～に先立って or ～前に.

• Meaning 1: Doing something “before” an important event/point in time (preparation/launch/introduction/opening…).
• Meaning 2: “Pioneering” ahead of rivals/other organizations in the same field.
• Often appears in news, press releases and slogans: emphasizes being in the lead.
• The subject is usually an organization/company/government; rarely used for an individual's everyday actions.
fields.notes:
• “先駆ける” = to go ahead, to pave the way; news reports like to use it to create a sense of leadership.
• The modifier form “Nに先駆けたN’” is very common in headlines: 「世界に先駆けた発表」.
• Does not combine directly with verbs; it must go through an event noun: “発売に先駆けて発表する”.
mistakes: Using it for small everyday actions (e.g. 朝食に先駆けて歯を磨く) → sounds exaggerated, unnatural.
Confusing it with ～に先立って: exam questions often ask you to pick the “pioneering/PR” nuance → choose “に先駆けて”.
It does not attach directly to a time clause (Vる＋前に) → it needs an event noun: ×出発に先駆けて vs 〇出発に先立って.

examples: If you ask him, this is just a coincidence.
According to experts, the cause apparently lies elsewhere.
In my parents' view, I'm apparently still a child.

fields.explain:
Used when quoting/presenting a point of view; often accompanied by a subjective evaluation (good/bad/unrealistic…).
The nuance can be slightly “snarky/distancing”: “according to them… (but it may not be true)”.
In everyday spoken language, “～に言わせると” is more natural; “～に言わせれば” is more formal/emphatic.

• Gives an evaluation/judgment “from N's point of view”. May imply “that is just how N sees it”.
• Often carries a distancing nuance, sometimes with a sense of rebuttal/skepticism/light mockery.
• Can be used with “私”: 私に言わせれば～ to emphasize a strong personal opinion.
fields.notes:
• Translate flexibly: “according to N”, “if you ask N”, “as far as N is concerned”. Depending on the context, keep a distancing or neutral nuance.
• Goes well with nouns for agents who make evaluations: 専門家・医者・教師・親・世間・当事者・本人…
• When the subject is “I”, use “私に言わせれば” to make it more subjective and emphasize a personal stance.
mistakes: Confusing it with “にとって”: “彼に言わせれば大切だ” ≠ “彼にとって大切だ”. One is an “opinion”, the other is “value for someone”.
Missing the distancing nuance: exam questions may build in a sense of skepticism → choose “に言わせれば/に言わせると” instead of “によると”.
Using it with inanimate things (×会社に言わせれば) → if it is an organization understood as “the representatives/the company side”, it is acceptable: 会社側に言わせれば…

examples: This disease is not limited to the elderly.
Online slander on social media is not something that only happens to celebrities.
Mistakes are not limited to newcomers.

fields.explain:
Placed after a noun to deny that something is “exclusive to/occurs only in N”.
Often accompanied by words of limitation such as だけ, ばかり to emphasize and then negate: Nだけに限ったことではない.
An objective nuance, used when making a general statement or broadening the scope of the discussion.
Not used directly with adjectives/verbs; if needed, nominalize the subject: 〜する人/〜な傾向/〜という現象+ に限ったことではない.

• “It is not something limited to N” → the phenomenon/matter does not only happen with N but is more widespread.
• Structure: 限る (to limit) → 限った (limited) + ことではない (is not a matter) → “not a matter limited to N”.
• Often used to counter the idea that “only N…”, broadening the scope to other targets.
• Neutral nuance, usable in both spoken and written language. Commonly seen in news/editorials.
fields.notes:
• When the subject is a person/group of people, use a noun phrase: 都市に住む人に限ったことではない.
• Often used with social topics: 少子化、物価高、ハラスメント、気候変動 など.
• Corresponding positive expression: Nに限った話ではない (not a story only about N).
mistakes: Using it directly with verbs/adjectives: × 忙しいに限ったことではない → ✔ 忙しい人に限ったことではない.
Confusing it with Nに限る (N is best/limited to N). The meaning is completely different.
Dropping “こと”: × Nに限ったではない → ✔ Nに限ったことではない.
Confusing its nuance with だけではない: exam questions may ask you to choose the more formal pattern → prefer に限ったことではない in serious written language.

examples: Receiving an award like this is the greatest honor.
I am terribly sorry to have troubled you when you are so busy; it was the height of rudeness.
To miss such a precious opportunity is extremely regrettable.
This reception room is the height of luxury.
We deeply regret having caused you such great inconvenience.
fields.explain:
Used to emphasize the highest degree through formal exaggeration.
Often appears in thanks/apologies, speeches and press releases:光栄の極み,遺憾の極み.
Not used in everyday conversation unless deliberately creating a “dramatic/rhetorical” nuance.
What follows can be だ/です/でございます to adjust the level of politeness.

• Expresses the “utmost/extreme” degree of a state or emotion: “N is at its peak”.
• Formal nuance with a strong rhetorical character; usually used in speeches and official documents.
• Limited combinations: tends toward abstract nouns or evaluations. Does not attach directly to adjectives; nominalization is needed.
• Different from 極まる/極まりない: の極み leans toward “naming something at its extreme” and is highly lexically fixed.
fields.notes:
• The phrase “遺憾の極み” is often seen in political statements/hearings.
• “贅沢の極み” can carry a nuance of praise or of sarcasm depending on the context.
• If you want a strong critical tone, consider “極まりない”: その発言は無責任極まりない。
mistakes: Using it directly with adjectives: incorrect. You do not say “嬉しいの極み” → correct: “感激の極み”.
Using it in casual speech sounds “over the top”. Choose 極まりない/とても… in everyday conversation.
Confusing it with の至り: “迷惑の至り” sounds forced; for negative things use “迷惑の極み”.

examples: It is the greatest honor to be invited to an occasion like this.
I am deeply moved by the support of so many people.
My rudeness the other day was the result of youthful folly.

fields.explain:
A humble/ceremonial nuance, suitable for official speeches, letters and congratulatory speeches.
Usually comes at the end of a sentence with です／でございます／に存じます to increase politeness.
“若気の至り” is also used in spoken language, but still carries a slight sense of excuse-making.

• Expresses an “utmost/extreme” degree, but leans toward the speaker's humble, polite expression.
• Common in formal thanks/congratulations/apologies; has a more classical tone than の極み.
• “若気の至り” gives youth as the reason excusing immature behavior.
• The range of nouns it combines with is limited; emotion/ceremonial nouns are preferred.
fields.notes:
• In formal letters, the fixed pattern まことに光栄の至りに存じます。 can be used.
• “恐悦至極/至りに存じます” is an archaic, highly formal form used in ceremonies.
• Do not overuse “若気の至り” to dodge responsibility in serious contexts.
mistakes: Using it with everyday negative nouns sounds unnatural: “迷惑の至り” → prefer “迷惑の極み”.
Using it in casual conversation sounds “overly solemn”.
Getting the keigo wrong: “至りに思います” is unnatural → “至りに存じます”.

rows: Used for both positive and negative; broader in nuance
Strongly critical tone, little ceremonial character

examples: Whatever the result, I want to value the process.
Whoever he is, he will have to follow the rules.
Whether or not we win the contract, let's submit a quote anyway.
Whether it succeeds or fails, the attempt was worth it.
Wherever the venue is, please be punctual.
Whatever the evaluation, report the facts calmly.
fields.explain:
Used to affirm a stance/standard that does not change.
Often used with commands/suggestions/volition: ～してください／～べきだ／～つもりだ.
More formal than ～にかかわらず／～を問わず, with a declarative character.

• “No matter how A turns out, B (stays the same).” Emphasizes that B is not affected by A.
• Formal style, used when stating principles/views/directions.
• The scope of A can be a result, circumstances, identity, place,...
fields.notes:
• An equivalent expression with a legal/regulatory nuance: ～のいかんにかかわらず.
• “は/が” before どうであれ: は for contrast/emphasis, が is more objective.
• Often used with pairs of opposites: 成功/失敗, 賛成/反対, 高い/安い.
mistakes: Using it for matters without multiple possible “hows” → unnatural. This pattern presupposes that A has several possibilities.
Attaching it to a purely descriptive clause (with no stance) → the meaning becomes weak: it should be followed by a clear request/view.
Confusing it with ～ても: ～はどうであれ is more formal and general, not used for momentary emotions.
